Energy Needs 
2.64 Energy self-sufficiency is a stated US national goal. In recent years, the Federal budget has included increasingly larger appropriations for research into such devices as fast-breeder nuclear reactors, large wind-driven electrical generators, solar collectors, and tidal wave generators. The nuclear reactors and tidal wave generators would be very large facilities, the energy from which would be distributed over existing electrical transmission networks. Wind turbines and solar collectors could be of various sizes, ranging from units to serve an individual household up to batteries of units to serve small towns. All of these devices are experimental and are possible long range solutions. At present they are either technically in the developmental stage of they are not economically feasible when compared to conventional methods of electrical generation.
2.65 For the short range, presently estimated to be approximately the remainder of the 20th century, less exotic methods must be used to satisfy the growing electrical demand. These include maximizing the efficiency of fuel combustion, developing new methods of coal, oil, and gas extraction, reducing requirements for cooling and heating in new houses, etc. At the same time the demand is increasing, it is necessary to decrease the rate at which the available (but limited) fuel resources are being depleted, not only for the fossil fuels, but also fur uranium which at one time was thought to be more or less unlimited. Unfortunately, whether the fuel is used for direct heating of homes and businesses, to fire furnaces, to operate vehicles, or to produce electric energy, the final result is the samedepletion of nonrenewable domestic resources continues unabated.
